# Settings (pianistpy.settings)

Numerical settings: the tested tiers and expert overrides.

class pianistpy.settings.Field(default, doc, quick=None)

One numerical setting: its value in each tier and what it controls.

Parameters:

default (bool, int, float or str) – Value in the default tier. Its type is the type of the field.

doc (str) – What the field controls.

quick (bool, int, float or str, optional) – Value in the quick tier. If omitted, the quick tier keeps the default
value: a cheaper value enters only once it has passed the tests.

value(tier)

Return the value of the field in a tier.

Parameters:

tier (str)

Return type:

Any

class pianistpy.settings.Settings(quick=False, write_anyway=False, **overrides)

Numerical settings of a computation.

A tier is a complete set of numerical settings that has been run through
the test battery and for which the package states the accuracy it
delivers. An expert may override single fields; the result then records
that it was not made with a tested tier and names the fields that differ.

Parameters:

quick (bool, optional) – Use the quick tier instead of the default tier.

write_anyway (bool, optional) – Return a result whose own check lies beyond the hard limit instead of
refusing it. The result carries the check’s verdict in its validation
report (tier "refused") and an AccuracyWarning is issued in
place of the refusal. For debugging a case the package cannot serve
at its stated accuracy; off by default. A physically invalid model
is refused regardless.

**overrides (mapping) – One mapping per group (inversion, truncation, sampling,
observables) of the fields to change within that group.

Variables:

tier (str) – Name of the tier the settings start from.

write_anyway (bool) – Whether a result beyond the hard limit is returned instead of refused.

overrides (mapping) – The fields changed from the tier, by group. Read only.

Examples

```
>>> Settings().tier
'default'
>>> Settings(quick=True).is_tested_tier
True
>>> Settings(inversion={"n_nodes": 256}).is_tested_tier
False
>>> Settings(inversion={"n_nodes": 256}).inversion["n_nodes"]
256
>>> Settings().truncation["ode_rtol"]
1e-11

```

property tier: str

Name of the tier the settings start from.

property write_anyway: bool

Whether a result beyond the hard limit is returned instead of refused.

property overrides: Mapping[str, Mapping[str, Any]]

The fields changed from the tier, by group.

property is_tested_tier: bool

Whether the settings are a tested tier with no field changed.

group(name)

Return the value of every field of one group.

Parameters:

name (str) – One of the groups inversion, truncation, sampling and
observables.

Returns:

values – The fields of the group with the values of the tier, each
replaced by its override where one was given. Read only.

Return type:

mapping

property inversion: Mapping[str, Any]

Settings of the inversion.

property truncation: Mapping[str, Any]

Settings of the truncation.

property sampling: Mapping[str, Any]

Settings of the particle sampling.

property observables: Mapping[str, Any]

Settings of the observables.

property losvd: Mapping[str, Any]

The fields of the LOSVD table and the aperture LOSVD.

resolved()

Return every field of every group with the value in force.

Return type:

dict[str, dict[str, Any]]

to_dict()

Return the settings as a plain dictionary.

Returns:

record – The tier and the overrides, in the form written to files, with
"write_anyway": True where that was asked. The numerical
settings alone determine a result, so numerical is what the
identity hashes.

Return type:

dict

numerical()

Return the tier and the overrides, the settings that determine a result.

Return type:

dict[str, Any]

# Superposition (pianistpy.superposition)

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/superposition.html

# Superposition (pianistpy.superposition)

Linear superposition of models that share one density.

pianistpy.superposition.mixture(weights, values, xp=np)

Return the weighted sum of per-component values, the weights normalized.

The one way a superposed model combines its components: a density, a
moment or a table read per component. Linear in the values, and in the
weights up to their normalization; with xp=jax.numpy the weights may
be traced, so a quantity of the mixture is differentiable in them.

Parameters:

weights (array-like, shape (n_components,)) – Positive weights; normalized here.

values (array-like, shape (n_components, ...)) – The value of each component.

xp (module, optional) – numpy, or jax.numpy for traced weights.

Returns:

value

Return type:

array, shape (…)

pianistpy.superposition.moments(model, r, n_nodes=None)

Return the second moments of a superposed model at radii r.

Parameters:

model (Model) – A superposed model (superpose), its components sharing one density.

r (array-like, shape (n,)) – Radii, in internal units.

n_nodes (int, optional) – Gauss-Legendre nodes of each component’s Jeans integral; the model’s
observables.n_jeans_nodes if omitted.

Returns:

moments – sigma_r2 and sigma_t2 of the mixture, beta_sigma its
anisotropy, and sigma_r2_components and beta_components (one
row per component), with the shape of r.

Return type:

dict

Notes

Each component’s radial dispersion is the Jeans integral of its
auxiliary density on the shared profile (radial_dispersion, the
Gauss-Legendre rule in ln(1 - K / P_0)); its components share the density,
so the moments of the mixture are the weighted sums
\(\sigma_r^2 = \sum_k w_k\sigma_{r,k}^2\),
\(\sigma_t^2 = 2\sum_k w_k(1-\beta_k)\sigma_{r,k}^2\) and
\(\beta_\sigma = 1 - \sigma_t^2 / (2\sigma_r^2)\).

References

Paper Eqs. (B42), (B43) [eqn:linearity_2, eqn:linearity_beta_1] and
eqn:beta_sigma_sup.

pianistpy.superposition.superpose(members)

Return the superposition of models that share one truncated pair.

Parameters:

members (mapping of Model to float) – Two or more models of one component each, every one built on the same
truncated profile (Method II children of one truncated parent), with
their weights. The weights must be positive; they are normalized to
sum to one, with a warning where they did not.

Returns:

model – One component per member, in the order given: the member’s component
with its mass the weight relative to the first member’s; its DF table
on its own energy grid (DfTable carries one grid per component); the
shared profile with the density split by weight; the members’ checks,
each at its worst over the members.

Return type:

Model

Raises:

InputError – If fewer than two members are given, a weight is not positive and
    finite, a member is not a single Method II component on a truncated
    profile, the members are built on different profiles, or their
    settings or units differ.

     On this page

# Units (pianistpy.units)

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/units.html

# Units (pianistpy.units)

Conversion from internal units to model and physical units.

class pianistpy.units.UnitFactors(rho_norm, mass_q, model_v, model_mass, model_rho, model_p, physical_r_pc=None, physical_v_kms=None, physical_mass_msun=None, physical_rho_msun_pc3=None, physical_p_kms2=None, physical_rho_0_msun_pc3=None)

Factors that convert internal units to model and to physical units.

A quantity in internal units is multiplied by the factor to obtain it in
the target units. The model units have \(G = M_0 = r_0 = 1\), with
\(M_0\) the mass inside the radius concentration times
\(r_0\).

Parameters:

rho_norm (float) – Normalization \(C\) of the density profile.

mass_q (float) – \(q = \mathcal{M}(c)/C\), the mass inside the concentration
radius in units of \(4\pi\rho_0 r_0^3\).

model_v (float) – Factors to the model units, for a speed, a mass, a density and a
potential.

model_mass (float) – Factors to the model units, for a speed, a mass, a density and a
potential.

model_rho (float) – Factors to the model units, for a speed, a mass, a density and a
potential.

model_p (float) – Factors to the model units, for a speed, a mass, a density and a
potential.

physical_r_pc (float or None) – Factors to parsecs, kilometers per second and solar masses.

physical_v_kms (float or None) – Factors to parsecs, kilometers per second and solar masses.

physical_mass_msun (float or None) – Factors to parsecs, kilometers per second and solar masses.

physical_rho_msun_pc3 (float or None) – Factors to solar masses per cubic parsec, and to the square of
kilometers per second.

physical_p_kms2 (float or None) – Factors to solar masses per cubic parsec, and to the square of
kilometers per second.

physical_rho_0_msun_pc3 (float or None) – The scale density \(\rho_0\) in solar masses per cubic parsec.

Notes

The physical factors are None unless both physical scales were given to
unit_factors.

class pianistpy.units.Units(system='internal', concentration=None, mass_0_msun=None, r_0_pc=None)

The unit system of a result and the scales that define it.

Parameters:

system ({"internal", "model", "physical"}) – "internal": \(G = \rho_0/C = r_0 = 1\). "model":
\(G = M_0 = r_0 = 1\). "physical": Astropy quantities.

concentration (float, optional) – Concentration \(c\) that defines \(M_0\) as the mass inside
\(c\,r_0\). Needed by the model and the physical systems.

mass_0_msun (float, optional) – \(M_0\) in solar masses. Needed by the physical system.

r_0_pc (float, optional) – Scale radius \(r_0\) in parsecs. Needed by the physical system.

Examples

```
>>> Units().system
'internal'
>>> Units.build("model", concentration=10.0).concentration
10.0

```

classmethod build(system, concentration=None, mass_0=None, r_0=None, r_vir=None)

Return the units of a system from the scales a user gives.

Parameters:

system ({"internal", "model", "physical"}) – The target system.

concentration (float, optional) – Concentration that defines \(M_0\).

mass_0 (float or astropy Quantity, optional) – \(M_0\); a float is in solar masses.

r_0 (float or astropy Quantity, optional) – The scale radius, or the radius \(c\,r_0\) in its place; a
float is in parsecs. One of the two for the physical system.

r_vir (float or astropy Quantity, optional) – The scale radius, or the radius \(c\,r_0\) in its place; a
float is in parsecs. One of the two for the physical system.

Returns:

units

Return type:

Units

factors(profile)

Return the conversion factors of these units for a density profile.

Parameters:

profile (DoublePowerLaw)

Return type:

UnitFactors

convert(kind, value, profile)

Return a quantity in internal units in the units of this object.

Parameters:

kind ({"length", "velocity", "mass", "density", "potential"}) – What the quantity is.

value (array-like) – The quantity, in internal units.

profile (DoublePowerLaw) – The density profile that fixes the normalization.

Returns:

converted – A plain array for the internal and the model systems, an Astropy
quantity for the physical system.

Return type:

array or astropy Quantity

to_dict()

Return the units as a plain dictionary.

Return type:

dict[str, Any]

classmethod from_dict(record)

Build the units from their dictionary form; internal if absent.

Parameters:

record (Mapping[str, Any] | None)

Return type:

Units

pianistpy.units.unit_factors(profile, concentration, mass_0_msun=None, r_0_pc=None)

Return the conversion factors of a profile.

Parameters:

profile (DoublePowerLaw) – The density profile, which fixes the normalization \(C\).

concentration (float) – Radius, in units of the scale radius \(r_0\), inside which the
mass \(M_0\) is defined. Positive.

mass_0_msun (float, optional) – \(M_0\) in solar masses.

r_0_pc (float, optional) – Scale radius \(r_0\) in parsecs.

Returns:

factors – The model-unit factors, and the physical factors if both mass_0_msun
and r_0_pc are given.

Return type:

UnitFactors

Notes

With \(\rho_{\rm w} = \rho_0/C\) the internal units are
\(M_{\rm W} = 4\pi\rho_{\rm w} r_0^3\) for mass and
\(v_{\rm W} = \sqrt{4\pi G\rho_{\rm w} r_0^2}\) for speed, and
\(M_0 = 4\pi\rho_0 r_0^3\,q\). Hence a speed is multiplied by
\((C q)^{-1/2}\), a mass and a potential by \((C q)^{-1}\), and a
density by \((4\pi C q)^{-1}\) to reach the model units.

References

Paper I, Section on units (labels ssec:Units, eqn:M_nor_1).

Examples

```
>>> factors = unit_factors(DoublePowerLaw.nfw(), concentration=10.0)
>>> factors.rho_norm
1.0
>>> round(factors.mass_q, 12) == round(math.log(11.0) - 10.0 / 11.0, 12)
True

```

     On this page

# Validation (pianistpy.validation)

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/validation.html

# Validation (pianistpy.validation)

Accuracy tiers and the validation report of a result.

class pianistpy.validation.Check(error, where=None, reason=None, source=None, excluded=None)

One check of a result: what was measured and where.

Parameters:

error (float) – The relative error the check measured.

where (float, optional) – The place of the largest error, in the variable the check runs over
(a radius or an energy). Absent where that has no meaning.

reason (str, optional) – Why the check was not judged, where it was not: such a check has no
error (NaN), its tier reads "not judged", and the result’s tier
is the worst of the checks that were.

source (str, optional) – Where a judged check read its input from another source than its
own, what it read and why; the error and the tier are as measured.

excluded (str, optional) – Where a judged check leaves part of its input unjudged, which part
and why; the error and the tier are those of the rest.

property level: int

Tier of the error, as returned by tier_level; 0 for a check not
judged, which leaves the result’s tier to the others.

property tier: str

Name of the tier of the error, or "not judged".

class pianistpy.validation.ValidationReport(keys, checks, parents_level=0)

The validation report of one result.

The report has a fixed set of keys for each kind of result and one
Check per key. It is not a log: nothing is appended to it, and a
derived result holds its own checks and the worst tier of its parents,
never a copy of their reports.

Parameters:

keys (tuple of str) – The keys this kind of result reports, in order.

checks (mapping of str to Check) – One check per key.

parents_level (int, optional) – Worst tier among the parents of the result.

property level: int

Worst tier of the result’s own checks and of its parents.

property tier: str

Name of the worst tier.

classmethod from_dict(record)

Build the report from its dictionary form.

Parameters:

record (Mapping[str, Any])

Return type:

ValidationReport

to_dict()

Return the report as a plain dictionary, in the order of its keys.

Return type:

dict[str, Any]

pianistpy.validation.announce(what, report, detail)

Say that a result lies above the goal; silent within it.

The one channel for every block: the package’s log (the pianistpy
logger, printed by default) and Python’s own warnings, as an
AccuracyWarning, so that a user can silence or escalate it with the
standard filter. Nothing is said within the goal; beyond the hard limit
the result is refused by its stage, not announced here.

Parameters:

what (str) – The result, named: "The sampler of 'nfw'".

report (ValidationReport) – Its report.

detail (str) – The checks above the goal with their errors and where they occur.

Return type:

None

pianistpy.validation.refuse_unless_asked(what, report, settings)

Refuse a result beyond the hard limit as the input of another.

A result whose report reads "refused" exists only because it was asked
for anyway (Settings(write_anyway=True)) or was read from a file that
holds one. It is consumed only under the same request: a sampler, a table
or a projection built on it carries its tier and says so.

Parameters:

what (str) – The input, named: "The model 'nfw'".

report (ValidationReport) – Its report.

settings (Settings) – The settings of the result being built from it.

Raises:

AccuracyError – If the report’s tier is "refused" and the settings do not ask for
    the result anyway.

Return type:

None

pianistpy.validation.tier_level(error)

Return the tier of a relative error.

Parameters:

error (float) – Relative error, non-negative. A value that is not a number counts as
beyond the hard limit.

Returns:

level – 0 within the goal, 1 within the ceiling, 2 within the hard limit,
3 beyond it.

Return type:

int

Examples

```
>>> [tier_level(e) for e in (1e-7, 1e-5, 1e-3, 1e-1, float("nan"))]
[0, 1, 2, 3, 3]

```

     On this page

# Technical notes

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/notes.html

# Technical notes

The technical notes are the online companion of the paper: the equations, derivations, conditions and bounds
that the paper does not print, and the numerical design of each stage. Every formula implemented in the package
cites them from its docstring by a number and a fixed key, as in Notes Eq. (I.5) [conditions]; the key never
changes, the number follows the notes.

The notes are published as a PDF with each release; the link is added with the 1.0.0 release. Rendering them
as pages of this manual is among the Upcoming features.


---

# Settings tables

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/settings.html

# Settings tables

Every numerical setting of the package is a declared field of one group, with its value in each tested tier and
one line on what it controls. The tables below are generated from the package’s own declaration at every build
of this manual, so they cannot lag the code. The settings container is pianistpy.Settings; a stage reads
its group and nothing else; an override of an undeclared field, of the wrong type or not positive is refused.

## inversion

Field

Default

Quick

What it controls

n_nodes

500

same

Gauss-Legendre nodes of the inversion integral.

n_grid_rows

1000

same

Rows of the linear middle zone of the inversion’s energy grid.

n_grid_tail_rows

3000

same

Rows of each logarithmic end zone of the inversion’s energy grid, toward the floor and toward the top.

grid_tail_extent

0.03

same

Extent of the energy grid’s end zones, as a fraction of the central potential.

table_nodes_per_decade

50

same

Nodes per decade of the energy grid below its floor, down to the table’s floor.

n_floor_nodes

240

same

Gauss-Legendre nodes in ln P of the completion below the table’s floor (a third of them, at least 40, near the floor).

## truncation

Field

Default

Quick

What it controls

n_source_nodes

500

same

Gauss-Legendre nodes of each of the two intervals of the quadrature of the auxiliary density on the source grid.

n_source_rows

12000

same

Rows of the source grid in the potential.

n_source_tail_rows

3000

same

Rows of each logarithmic tail of the source grid, toward the floor and toward the top (at most a third of the rows).

source_tail_extent

0.03

same

Largest extent of the source grid’s tails, as a fraction of the grid’s top (the tails take at most a hundredth of the top).

source_tail_floor

1.20401e-08

same

Smallest start of the source grid’s lower tail and smallest extent of its upper tail, as fractions of the grid’s top.

quadrature_split

0.9

same

Fraction of the potential where the first interval of the source quadrature ends.

quadrature_stretch

2

same

Power k of the second interval’s map Q = P - u^k, where the kernel’s exponent is not negative.

ode_rtol

1e-11

same

Relative tolerance of the Poisson integration.

ode_atol

1e-11

same

Absolute tolerance of the Poisson integration.

n_rows_inner

500

same

Rows of the Poisson solve’s grid inside the inner zone.

n_rows_outer

59500

same

Rows of the Poisson solve’s grid outside the inner zone.

log10_r_min

-9

same

Logarithm of the Poisson solve’s innermost radius.

log10_r_max

12

same

Logarithm of the Poisson solve’s outermost radius; a run raises it until the potential there is below half the floor, and the result states the value it used.

continuation_start

0.01

same

Fraction of the central potential below which a truncated model’s last rows are re-solved on a grid geometric in R_t - r.

continuation_rows_per_decade

1200

same

Rows per decade of R_t - r of the edge continuation.

continuation_floor_fraction

0.02

same

The edge continuation’s last row, as a fraction of the floor.

profile_bin_decades

0.1

same

Width in decades of the potential of the profile’s row-count bins.

profile_rows_per_decade

1000

same

Fewest rows per decade of the potential (and of the depth) that the profile keeps at its two ends; the fills supply the rest.

## sampling

Field

Default

Quick

What it controls

n_rows

512

same

Rows in potential of the speed table to start from: the rows are refined until the table’s own error across rows is under the goal.

n_rows_max

4075

same

Most rows of the speed table: no refinement passes this count.

n_nodes

2048

512

Nodes of each row of the speed table.

n_speed_intervals

200

same

Intervals in the scaled speed of the distribution integrated on each row of the speed table.

n_gauss_legendre

16

8

Gauss-Legendre nodes of each panel of the speed integrals.

panels_per_decade

8

same

Panels per decade of the local variable where the speed integrals refine toward the two ends of a row and inside each interval.

speed_low_refined

1e-09

same

Smallest scaled speed refined in panels; below it the density is its power law in the speed, integrated in closed form.

edge_refined

1e-12

same

Distance from the edge of the speed support, relative to the edge, down to which panels refine; below it the DF’s rule below its table is integrated in closed form.

radius_edge_refined

1e-10

same

Smallest enclosed-mass fraction beyond a radius that the radius table of a model with a sharp edge resolves in nodes; beyond it the mass follows its power law in the distance from the edge.

n_radius_nodes

2048

same

Nodes of the radius table.

n_angle_nodes

1024

same

Nodes of each half of the angle table, uniform in the logarithm of the cumulative probability from its end.

draw_block

262144

same

Particles drawn at once: a draw runs over blocks of this many, so its working memory is one block’s (about 0.75 kB a particle, 2**18 particles about 0.2 GB) above its outputs, whatever the count; the particles are the same at any block size.

row_error_goal

1e-06

0.0001

Error across rows at which the speed table’s refinement stops (its rows double until the table’s own error is under it, or n_rows_max is reached).

tail_mass_min

1e-18

same

Smallest tabulated cumulative probability at either end of a table: a uniform double reaches 2**-53, so a draw never reads beyond it.

## observables

Field

Default

Quick

What it controls

n_radii

10000

500

Projected radii of the projection table before its certificate adds rows, logarithmic from the innermost row to the edge.

profile_tolerance

1e-07

1e-06

Relative error of sigma_r at which the radial dispersion’s rows stop being added: every interval’s midpoint reads within it. A tenth of the goal, the profile’s share of the error of what is projected from it.

n_profile_start

100

same

Logarithmic radii the radial dispersion starts from, from the innermost row to the edge, before rows are added to its tolerance.

n_jeans_nodes

500

Gauss-Legendre nodes of a row’s own Jeans integral of the radial dispersion (the superposition’s); the observables’ profile sums panels between its rows instead, their nodes doubled until sigma_r moves by less than profile_tolerance.

# Names and paper symbols

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/symbols.html

# Names and paper symbols

The package’s names follow the paper’s notation: a quantity that has a symbol in the paper or the technical notes
is named <family>_<symbol>, the family saying what kind of quantity it is and the rest being the paper’s symbol
or subscript in lower case. A truncated quantity (hatted in the paper) takes the suffix _trunc, the
untruncated one the bare name. Every docstring gives the paper’s symbol beside the name the first time it
describes it.

Family

Prefix

Names

Paper

density and its parameters

rho_

rho, rho_aux, rho_alpha, rho_beta, rho_gamma, rho_norm

\(\varrho\), \(\varrho_{\rm aux}\), \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\), \(C\)

anisotropy

beta_

beta_c, beta_sigma, beta_sup

\(\beta_{\rm c}\), \(\beta_\sigma\), \(\beta_{\rm sup}\)

radii

r_

r, r_a, r_t, r_2d, r_off, r_ape

\(R\), \(R_{\rm a}\), \(R_{\rm t}\), \(R_{\rm 2D}\), \(R_{\rm off}\), \(R_{\rm ape}\)

relative potential

p_

p, p_0

\(P\), \(P_0\)

energy-like variables

k_, q_

k, k_t, q, q_min, q_0

\(\mathcal{K}\), \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t}\), \(\mathcal{Q}\), \(\mathcal{Q}_{\rm min}\), \(\mathcal{Q}_0\)

distribution function

df_

df, df_k

\(F\), \(F_\mathcal{K}\)

mass

mass_

mass, mass_t, mass_vir

\(\mathcal{M}\), \(M_{\rm t}\), \(M_{\rm vir}\)

order of the inversion

order_

order_m, order_n

\((m, n)\)

velocities and dispersions

v_, sigma_

v_r, v_t, v_los, v_esc, sigma_r, sigma_t, sigma_los

\(V_r\), \(V_t\), \(V_{\rm los}\), \(V_{\rm esc}\), \(\sigma_r\), \(\sigma_t\), \(\sigma_{\rm los}\)

probability densities

pdf_

pdf_x, pdf_phi

\(p_x\), \(p_\varphi\)

Where the paper’s letter cannot be used, a word is fixed: the normalization \(C\) of the density is
rho_norm (rho_c would read as a central density), and the concentration \(c\) is concentration.
The letter c alone is never a name; as a subscript it means central (beta_c). The quantities of the
truncated model carry the suffix: p_trunc, df_trunc, rho_trunc, mass_trunc.

## Derived names

What

Form

Example

logarithm of a quantity

ln_, log10_ prefix

ln_r, log10_df

derivative

d<y>_d<x>, the order as a digit

drho_dp, d2rho_dp2

count

n_ prefix

n_nodes, n_rows

index

i_ prefix

i_split

quadrature nodes and weights

_nodes, _weights suffix

k_nodes, k_weights

tabulated values on a grid

_grid suffix

r_grid, df_grid

boolean

is_, has_ prefix

is_truncated, has_tail

The three unit systems are named internal (the dimensionless normalization of Widrow 2000, in which the
scale radius and the central potential of the untruncated profile are 1), model (\(G = M_0 = r_0 = 1\))
and physical (through Astropy); see Units.

# Install

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/start/install.html

# Install

```
pip install pianistpy

```

PIANISTpy needs Python 3.10 or later and runs on Linux, macOS and Windows.

## Requirements

The dependencies are installed by pip with the package. Two lists are kept with every release: the versions the
release was developed and tested with, and the oldest versions that pass the full test suite.

Package

Minimum (oldest that passes the suite)

Python

3.11

3.10 (the oldest with a JAX 0.6 wheel; the suite is run on 3.11)

NumPy

2.4

2.3.0

1.17

1.15.0

3.15

3.11.0

7.2

6.1.0

mpmath

1.4

1.1.0

SymPy

1.14

1.2

JAX

0.9.2

0.6.0

Diffrax

0.7.2

0.7.1

Optimistix

0.1.0

0.1.0

The minimum list is measured one package at a time with the others at their newest, and then all the minimum
versions together as one environment, which passes the suite; the standard list is the environment of the
release. Astropy below 7.2 needs NumPy below 2.4 (older Astropy calls a function NumPy 2.4 removed).

## JAX and the GPU

The package runs on the CPU everywhere and takes a GPU where the installed JAX supports one; nothing is set by
the user. JAX’s CUDA builds are for Linux: on Windows the GPU is reached through the Windows Subsystem for Linux
(or a Linux virtual machine) with the Linux wheels, and a native Windows Python runs the CPU-only mode. A GPU and
a CPU give results that differ at rounding on the kernels; the accuracy goal holds on both, and each file
records the backend that made it. To force one or the other, see Runtime options.

Only the main process uses the card: the worker processes of the observables’ pools run on the CPU. A card in the
Exclusive_Process compute mode (nvidia-smi --query-gpu=compute_mode --format=csv shows it), common on shared
clusters, serves one process, so where another process already holds it the package cannot reach it, and JAX’s
error begins Unable to initialize backend 'cuda'. Free the card, share it through an MPS daemon
(nvidia-cuda-mps-control -d), or run in the CPU-only mode.

A card speeds up the sampler and nothing else. The sampler’s speed table builds in 0.6 to 6.6 s on the card against
4.6 to 40 s on 8 cores, and drawing is faster on the card from about ten thousand particles, three to five times
from a hundred thousand. The DF’s Poisson solve is a serial ODE: where the package runs on a card, so does the
solve, and each step costs about a millisecond of launch latency, 50 to 200 times the CPU’s wall, so a model is
solved fastest in the CPU-only mode. The rows of the line-of-sight velocity table run in the worker pool on the CPU
whatever the platform, so a card does not shorten the table’s build (the two columns below differ by the main
process’s share and the node’s load), and reading a built table (the LOSVD, pdf_v) takes the CPU’s wall. At the
quick tier the table’s build ran out of the card’s 12 GB, so the quick tier’s observables were measured on the CPU
only. The walls below are from one 32-core node (AMD Threadripper PRO 5975WX) and one RTX 3080 Ti. The solve’s are
the medians of five reruns of 37 solves of 21 truncated models, in two groups by their step count. The speed
table’s are the steady builds of six members (512 to 1,021 rows) at the default tier, on 8 of the node’s cores. The
sampling’s and the observables’ are on an NFW model (beta_c 0.25, concentration 10) and a truncated Hernquist model
(Osipkov-Merritt Type I, beta_c -0.25, R_a 10, K_t 0.05); each is the median of three calls after a warm one, except
the table’s build, which is the first and the second build in one process.

Stage

RTX 3080 Ti

0.66 to 1.55 s

# What PIANISTpy does

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/start/overview.html

# What PIANISTpy does

Density profiles. Any double power law in its three slopes, with the Navarro-Frenk-White, Hernquist and
Plummer profiles as named presets.

Velocity anisotropy. Isotropic, constant, Osipkov-Merritt, and the generalized Osipkov-Merritt (Cuddeford)
models, radially biased (Type I) or tangentially biased (Type II).

Distribution functions. The distribution function (DF) of each model, from the analytic inversion of its
density, returned whether or not it is physical, with a statement of where it is not.

Truncation in phase space. Method I truncates a model’s own DF at an energy you give, or at the energy that
yields a target mass or a target radius. Method II gives a new anisotropy to a density that is already
truncated.

Particles. Positions and velocities drawn by inversion, with no rejection step, and reproducible particle
by particle.

Observables. Intrinsic and line-of-sight velocity dispersions, line-of-sight velocity distributions, and
their averages over apertures.

Superposition. Distribution functions inverted from one truncated density (Method II children of one
parent), combined with positive weights that sum to one into one equilibrium model.

Inference. The log-likelihood of a model against data, as a JAX function of the components’ weights and
the scales of the units.


---

# Quick start

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/start/quickstart.html

# Quick start

The example of the paper’s first figure: an NFW halo with a constant velocity anisotropy of 0.25, truncated in
phase space at the virial mass of a concentration-10 halo, presented as a Milky Way-mass halo.

```
import pianistpy as pp
import astropy.units as u

# an untruncated NFW density profile with a constant velocity anisotropy of 0.25
halo = pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.nfw(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25))

# the untruncated distribution function
df = pp.compute_df(halo)

# Method I: truncate it so that the truncated mass equals the virial mass of the
# untruncated NFW halo of concentration 10 (the mass inside 10 scale radii)
model = pp.truncate(df, pp.Truncation(mass_t=1.0, concentration=10))

# physical units: a halo of 1e12 solar masses with R_vir = c * r_0 = 200 kpc
model = model.to("physical", mass_0=1e12 * u.Msun, r_0=20 * u.kpc)

# draw ten million equal-mass particles centered at the origin and write them to a file
particles = pp.Sampler(model).sample(10_000_000, seed=1)
particles.write("NFW_Const0p25_Mt1e12_PARIC.h5")

# the line-of-sight velocity dispersion at three projected radii
sigma = pp.sigma_los(model, [2, 20, 100] * u.kpc)

```

pp.solve(halo, truncation) runs the two steps at once.

Every result carries a validation report with its accuracy tier, and a model is always a valid equilibrium; what
the package returns, flags and refuses is on one page, Flags and refusals.
